result: EDA-KO pigs were successfully generated using CRISPR/Cas9 targeting exon 4 of the EDA gene, which encodes the collagen domain required for proper gland development. All piglets from four litters had loss-of-function indels, with birth weights similar to wild-type controls and no observed sex differences despite EDA being X-linked.
evaluation: Claims C42-C48 and C123-C126 collectively describe the generation and characterization of EDA-KO pigs. The molecular rationale (targeting the collagen domain), genetic editing approach (CRISPR/Cas9), sequencing confirmation (Figure 1), and phenotypic characterization (birth weights, lack of sex differences) provide strong converging evidence. The biochemical mechanism linking collagen domain mutations to loss of function is well-supported by prior literature.

result: EDA-KO pigs exhibited characteristic ectodermal dysplasia phenotypes including sparse hair in linear patterns, bald patches on the head, lack of eyelid hair while retaining eyelashes, and loss of glands in multiple tissues. These phenotypes are consistent with those reported in other animals with ectodysplasin pathway mutations.
evaluation: Claims C50-C53 and C57 describe the physical phenotypes of EDA-KO pigs, supported by photographic evidence (Figure 2) and histological data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1). The consistency with prior animal models (C53) strengthens the interpretation that these are bona fide EDA loss-of-function phenotypes.

result: EDA-KO pigs completely lacked submucosal glands throughout all conducting airways (trachea, bronchi, bronchioles), while wild-type pigs showed the expected proximal-to-distal gradient of SMG distribution similar to humans.
evaluation: Claims C2, C54-C56 describe the primary anatomical phenotype. Histological evidence (Figure 3A-B) demonstrates complete absence of SMGs in EDA-KO airways across all airway levels with quantitative analysis showing 0% circumference with SMGs in EDA-KO versus significant percentages in wild-type (p<0.05 for trachea, secondary and segmental bronchi). This is the critical phenotype enabling all subsequent functional studies.

result: Surface epithelial cells in EDA-KO airways showed normal expression and localization of mucins MUC5AC and MUC5B, and normal distribution of ciliated cells marked by β-tubulin IV, indicating that loss of SMGs did not grossly alter surface epithelial differentiation.
evaluation: Claims C58-C60 are supported by immunofluorescence data (Figure 4A-B) showing similar staining patterns for MUC5AC, MUC5B, and β-tubulin IV in EDA-KO and wild-type airways. This control experiment is important for establishing that observed functional defects are attributable to SMG loss rather than secondary effects on surface epithelia.

result: Airway surface liquid from EDA-KO pigs had significantly reduced bacterial killing capacity compared to wild-type (killing <25% vs ~50% of S. aureus at 1 min), indicating that SMGs contribute substantially to antimicrobial activity on the proximal airway surface through production of antimicrobials including lysozyme and lactoferrin.
evaluation: Claims C3, C4, C61-C64 describe reduced antimicrobial activity in EDA-KO pigs. The in vivo bacterial killing assay (Figure 5) shows statistically significant reduction (p<0.0012). The assay design (bacteria tethered to grids for 1 min) appropriately isolates antimicrobial activity from MCT and phagocytosis. The interpretation that SMGs produce antimicrobials (C4, C61) is well-supported by prior literature and consistent with the observed phenotype.

result: Wild-type pigs produced hundreds of mucus strands that emerged from SMG ducts and swept across the airway surface, while EDA-KO airways had essentially no mucus strands despite normal ciliary beating. Mucus strands are composed primarily of MUC5B produced by SMG acinar cells and function to bind particulate material.
evaluation: Claims C5, C65-C72 describe the loss of mucus strands in EDA-KO airways. Confocal microscopy data (Figure 6A-B, Videos 1-2) show dramatic reduction in strand counts (p=0.0016) while ciliary beat frequency remained normal (Figure 6C, p=0.4351). This establishes that mucus strand production is SMG-dependent and not due to ciliary dysfunction. The molecular composition (MUC5B) is supported by prior literature (C65-C66).

result: In ex vivo tracheal preparations, mucus strands in wild-type airways wrapped around and transported metallic spheres to the airway edge, while in EDA-KO airways lacking mucus strands, spheres moved less frequently and tended to spin in place rather than being cleared.
evaluation: Claims C73-C75 describe the functional role of mucus strands in particle transport using an ex vivo sphere tracking assay. Data (Figure 6D-E, Videos 3-4) show significantly fewer spheres moved >1 mm in EDA-KO airways (p=0.0061). The qualitative observation of spheres spinning versus being transported provides mechanistic insight into how mucus strands initiate and sustain particle movement.

result: Under basal (unstimulated) conditions in vivo, microdisks showed reduced movement in EDA-KO versus wild-type pigs, with significantly decreased percentage of time in motion (p=0.0238), though speed when moving was similar and clearance showed only a non-significant trend toward reduction.
evaluation: Claims C76-C80 describe basal MCT measured by CT tracking of tantalum microdisks (Figure 7A-D, Videos 5-6). The percentage of time in motion was significantly reduced (p=0.0238), but speed and clearance were not significantly different. This suggests SMGs contribute to MCT even under basal conditions, though the effect is more modest than under stimulated conditions. The statistical analysis is appropriate.

result: After methacholine stimulation to activate SMG secretion, wild-type pigs showed robust microdisk movement and clearance, while EDA-KO pigs had significantly reduced time in motion (p=0.0238) and failed to clear any microdisks from the lung (p=0.0238), demonstrating that SMG loss severely impairs stimulated mucociliary transport in vivo.
evaluation: Claims C81-C85 describe stimulated MCT using the same CT-based assay. The data (Figure 7, Videos 7-8) show dramatic impairment in EDA-KO pigs with statistically significant differences in time in motion and clearance (both p=0.0238). The contrast between basal and stimulated conditions highlights the importance of SMG secretion for effective MCT. Sample sizes are small (n=6 WT, n=3 EDA-KO) but effects are large and consistent.

result: Four hours after S. aureus aerosol challenge, EDA-KO pigs had ~10,000-fold more bacteria in tracheal washes (p=0.0016) and ~100-fold more in BAL (p=0.0186) compared to wild-type, while distal lung homogenates showed no significant difference. This suggests EDA-KO pigs are particularly impaired at eliminating bacteria in large SMG-containing airways.
evaluation: Claims C7, C86-C91, C94 describe the bacterial challenge experiment (Figure 8). The data show statistically significant increases in bacterial burden in proximal airways (trachea, BAL) but not distal lung, supporting the interpretation that SMGs are critical for bacterial clearance in regions where they are normally present. The speculation about distal airway defenses being spared (C91) is appropriately qualified. The 4-hour timepoint is reasonable but additional timepoints would strengthen conclusions.

result: The study provides direct in vivo and ex vivo evidence that SMGs are required for normal antimicrobial activity and mucociliary transport, two critical respiratory host defenses. SMGs protect the lung by contributing to bacterial killing and producing mucus strands that facilitate MCT in cartilaginous airways.
evaluation: Claims C8-C9, C92-C93, C95, C118-C122 represent the main conclusions synthesizing all experimental findings. These conclusions are well-supported by the convergence of evidence from bacterial killing assays (reduced antimicrobial activity), ex vivo MCT assays (loss of mucus strands and sphere transport), in vivo MCT assays (impaired microdisk clearance), and bacterial challenge (impaired bacterial eradication). The study successfully addresses the stated hypothesis and fills a significant knowledge gap.

result: The authors propose that evolutionary advantages of SMGs include expanding the number of epithelial cells producing antimicrobials and mucus, and enabling rapid on-demand secretion via vagal cholinergic innervation, which could be critical for responding to acute challenges like aspiration, irritants, and pathogens.
evaluation: Claims C96-C98 present interpretations about the evolutionary advantages of SMGs. C96 and C97 are supported by prior anatomical and physiological literature. C98 is appropriately framed as speculation ('could be') and is a reasonable inference from the data, though it remains untested in this study.

result: Mucus strands bind to large particles and transmit forces from beating cilia to initiate and sustain particle transport. Disrupting mucus strand architecture by breaking disulfide crosslinks impairs MCT, suggesting that both the abundance and unique architecture of SMG-derived mucus strands are important for host defense.
evaluation: Claims C99-C101 synthesize findings from this study with prior work. C99 is supported by the sphere transport data (Figure 6D-E) and prior studies. C100 cites prior work showing that disrupting strand structure impairs MCT. C101 is a reasonable inference integrating these observations. The mechanistic link between strand architecture and function is well-supported.

result: The anatomical distribution of SMGs correlates with airway size across species, with SMGs present in large airways where airflow deposits large particles and absent in small airways that large particles don't reach. This relationship holds across mammals, with variations (e.g., smaller SMG volume in horses) potentially reflecting differences in particle filtration by nasal structures.
evaluation: Claims C102-C110 discuss comparative anatomy and functional implications. The anatomical observations (C102, C105-C107) are supported by cited literature. The functional interpretation linking SMG distribution to particle deposition patterns (C103-C104) is reasonable and consistent with airway physiology. The speculation about horses (C108-C110) is appropriately qualified and represents a plausible hypothesis.

result: SMGs contribute to host defense under basal (non-stimulated) conditions, as evidenced by decreased bacterial killing, reduced MCT measures, and impaired bacterial eradication in EDA-KO pigs without cholinergic stimulation. This is consistent with prior studies showing SMGs produce small amounts of mucus basally.
evaluation: Claims C111-C113 address the role of SMGs under basal conditions. The bacterial killing assay (Figure 5) and basal MCT measurements (Figure 7) were performed without stimulation, and both showed deficits in EDA-KO pigs. The bacterial challenge (Figure 8) was also performed without exogenous stimulation. These data support the conclusion that SMGs function basally, consistent with prior literature (C113).

result: The authors predict that impaired host defenses in EDA-KO pigs will lead to development of lung disease over time, a prediction supported by limited reports of respiratory symptoms in humans with hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia (HED).
evaluation: Claims C114-C115 represent predictions about future disease development. While the prediction is logical given the observed host defense defects, it remains untested as the study examined only newborn pigs (2-8 days old). The supporting evidence from HED patients (C115) is acknowledged as limited. Longitudinal studies would be needed to confirm this prediction.

result: In chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, some forms of asthma, and cystic fibrosis, SMG volume can increase several-fold and mucus production is abundant, raising questions about whether these diseases would be more or less severe without SMGs.
evaluation: Claims C116-C117 cite prior literature about SMG changes in disease states and pose a question for future research. The cited observations about SMG hypertrophy and mucus overproduction in disease are well-established. The question about disease severity without SMGs is appropriately framed as an open question rather than a conclusion.

result: EDA-KO piglets exhibited persistent sneezing beginning within hours of birth, which was the only observed behavioral difference from wild-type piglets.
evaluation: Claim C49 describes a behavioral phenotype. While this observation is clearly stated, no quantitative data or mechanistic explanation is provided. Sneezing could reflect irritation due to impaired mucus clearance or other factors. This observation is interesting but underdeveloped in the manuscript.

result: The introduction establishes background knowledge about airway surface liquid, SMG anatomy and function, limitations of prior models, the ectodysplasin pathway, and the rationale for using pigs as a model system. This includes the gap in knowledge that SMG function has not been directly tested in vivo.
evaluation: Claims C1, C10-C41 represent background knowledge and rationale from the introduction. These claims are appropriately supported by extensive citations to prior literature. The identification of the knowledge gap (C16-C17) effectively motivates the study. The choice of pigs as a model (C30-C35) is well-justified based on anatomical and physiological similarities to humans.
